content.content:
**Originating element of `::view-transition`:** The spec states its "originating element is the document’s [document element](...)", and that all view transition pseudo-elements are selected from their "ultimate originating element, the document element". So it hangs off the root element, and selectors are written as `:root::view-transition-group(name)` rather than nesting off `::view-transition`.

**Tree structure (parenthood):** Because these are tree-abiding pseudos in a pseudo-element tree, "its originating pseudo-element is its parent." The hierarchy is `::view-transition` → `::view-transition-group()` → `::view-transition-image-pair()` → `::view-transition-old()` / `::view-transition-new()`.

**Inheritance:** The page above does not include an explicit normative statement about general property or custom-property inheritance from the root element into `::view-transition`. What it does show is inheritance being used deliberately for animation timing in the UA stylesheet, where `::view-transition-image-pair(*)`, `::view-transition-old(*)`, and `::view-transition-new(*)` set `animation-duration: inherit`, `animation-fill-mode: inherit`, `animation-delay: inherit`, etc. The rationale given is to "Inherit animation timing through the tree so that by default, the animation timing set on a ::view-transition-group() will dictate the animation timing of all its descendants."

That implies inheritance does flow parent-to-child along the pseudo-element tree (group → image-pair → old/new), and by extension from the document element into `::view-transition`, since parentage in the pseudo tree is defined by the originating relationship. But the truncated content here doesn't spell that out for arbitrary inherited properties or custom properties — for a definitive answer you'd want the full spec text or `[css-pseudo-4]`, which the document notes may eventually host these tree-of-pseudo-element definitions.

content.text:
Done. Builds and typechecks clean.

## What I did

Next 16.4-canary turned out to have first-class support for this, so no experimental flag was needed: `ViewTransition`/`addTransitionType` ship in the React build Next bundles for the App Router (the `experimental.viewTransition` flag is gone from the config schema), it works in Server Components over the RSC wire, and `<Link>` has a `transitionTypes` prop that feeds `React.addTransitionType`.

**Shared element morph** — `lib/transitions.ts:12` derives one `view-transition-name` per product. The grid thumbnail (`app/ProductGrid.tsx:25`) and the detail hero (`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx:49`) both use it, so React pairs them across the navigation and morphs rather than fading each independently. Since the thumbnail is 4:3 and the hero 1:1, the snapshots are pinned to the group box with `object-fit: cover` — without that, a snapshot keeps its natural height while the group's width animates and the image shears. I also gave `.product-image` its own top border-radius: it renders identically today (the card already clips it) but a snapshotted element is lifted out of its ancestors' clipping, so it needed the radius itself to morph into the rounded hero.

**Directional slide** — one `<ViewTransition>` in the root layout around a `.page` wrapper. The layout never unmounts, so a navigation arrives as an *update* there, which drives the slide; the wrapper exists to hold the box geometry steady across routes so the slide isn't fighting a width/height morph. Links tag direction (`nav-forward` from the grid, `nav-back` from the back link) and a per-type class map picks the keyframes.

**Suspense reveal** — `<ViewTransition>` around each boundary, which is what makes React animate the fallback→content swap. Deliberately *no* size override here: letting the snapshots keep their natural height is what makes the height change read as a morph rather than a stretch.

**Reduced motion** — everything above is movement or scaling, so it all goes: group animations off (each group snaps to final geometry), replaced by a 120ms opacity-only cross-fade. I also stopped the existing skeleton `pulse`, since that's motion too.

Two things worth knowing:

- **I could not verify the animations in a browser.** The sandbox has no package manager, so Chromium is missing 18 shared libraries and won't launch. What I did verify: production build + typecheck, all routes 200 (404 still 404), the RSC payload carrying the correct paired names and transition types, and — the failure I was most worried about — that the CSS minifier didn't silently drop the `::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements. It didn't. The visual timing/feel is unconfirmed and worth an eyeball.
- **Browser back/forward buttons get a cross-fade, not a directional slide.** Next only calls `addTransitionType` for navigations it initiates from `Link`/`router`; popstate has no hook to inject a type, so those fall through to the `default` class. The in-page "← Back to products" link *is* directional. Wiring up true popstate direction would need history-index tracking — say the word if you want it.

One thing I left alone deliberately: the detail page's root is a bare `<div>` while the home page uses `<main>`, so the detail page renders full-bleed with no padding. That's a pre-existing layout inconsistency, and changing it would visibly restyle a page you didn't ask me to touch — the `.page` wrapper makes the transition read correctly either way.
